title: What Do I Know?
author: Michel de Montaigne
wiifm: Montaigne read the Stoics, loved them, and then noticed that their perfect, unshakeable sage did not describe any human being he had ever met, least of all himself. So he invented a new way of writing in order to tell the truth instead. We follow him from a baby sent to live with peasants, through a friendship that ended in grief, a near-fatal riding accident and a tower full of books, to the mayor's office of a city at war. You will come away with a working scepticism, a habit of testing advice against your own life, and the essay itself.

ch.h: A baby sent to the village
b: Michel Eyquem was born on 28 February 1533 at the family château of Montaigne, east of Bordeaux. The nobility was new. His great-grandfather had been a Bordeaux merchant in wine and salted fish who bought the estate, and the family had climbed into the minor nobility within living memory. His mother came from a wealthy merchant family that was probably of Spanish Jewish origin, converted to Christianity.

His father, Pierre, had enthusiasms, and his son was the main one. The baby was sent to be nursed in a nearby village among poor peasant families, so that he would feel close to the people who worked the land. Back at the château he was woken each morning by a musician, on the theory that sudden waking harmed a child's tender brain.

Most extraordinary of all, Pierre decided his son would speak Latin as his first language. He hired a German tutor who spoke no French, and ordered the whole household, parents and servants included, to speak to the boy only in Latin. When he arrived at the Collège de Guyenne in Bordeaux at six, his Latin was so fluent that, he says, his teachers were nervous of speaking it with him.

It was an experiment in raising a perfect scholar, and in a sense it worked. Montaigne read the ancients all his life as if they were living friends. But it also left him with a lifelong awareness of the gap between the theories adults impose on a person and what that person actually turns out to be. That gap would become his subject.
ch.cap: A musician wakes young Michel as his Latin tutor waits

ch.h: Because it was he, because it was I
b: He studied law, probably at Toulouse, and became a magistrate, first at Périgueux and then in the parlement of Bordeaux, the region's high court. There, around 1558 or 1559, he met a fellow magistrate a few years older called Étienne de La Boétie. La Boétie had already written, as a young man, a fierce short treatise on voluntary servitude, arguing that tyrants rule only because people consent to obey them.

They became friends at once and completely. The friendship lasted only four or five years. In August 1563 La Boétie fell ill, probably with dysentery or plague, and died at thirty-two, with Montaigne at his bedside for days. Montaigne wrote his father a long letter describing the death in detail.

Years later, in the essay Of Friendship, he tried to explain what they had been to each other, and could not. If pressed to say why he loved him, he wrote, he could only answer: because it was he, because it was I. No reasons. No mechanism. And he refuses every comfort. He does not say he was lucky to have had it. He says that compared with those years, the rest of his life has been smoke and dark night.

Some scholars think the Essays exist because La Boétie died: that the book is a substitute for the conversation, a friend made of paper. Whether or not that is the cause, it is part of the effect. Montaigne writes to his reader as a confidant, not an audience, and the intimacy that makes him feel so modern may be grief looking for somewhere to go.

It also sets him against the Stoics. Epictetus told you to remind yourself, when you kiss someone you love, that they are mortal. Montaigne had loved fully and lost anyway, and decided the protection was not worth what it cost the loving.
ch.cap: Montaigne keeps vigil at his dying friend's bedside

b: Some time in the late 1560s, the exact year is uncertain, Montaigne went out riding near home on a small, easy horse. One of his own servants, a big strong man on a powerful horse, decided to show off by galloping up the path, and crashed straight into him. Montaigne was thrown ten or twelve paces and landed on his back, senseless, his sword flung away, his horse knocked flat. His men thought he was dead. He was coughing up blood.

They carried him home. On the way he began to come round, and what fascinated him for the rest of his life was what it had felt like from the inside. It was not agony. It was not terror. He felt a gentle drifting, as if letting himself slip away, and found it almost pleasant. He remembered tearing at his doublet with his hands without knowing why. The pain came only later, as he recovered.

He wrote it up years afterwards in an essay called Of Practice, and drew a conclusion that cut across everything his classical reading had taught him. The ancients had told men to spend their lives preparing for death. His own evidence suggested dying needed no preparation at all. If you do not know how to die, he later wrote, do not worry: nature will tell you what to do on the spot.

That is Montaigne's method in miniature. Something happens. He notices what it was actually like, as opposed to what the books said it should be like. He reports the difference. Across more than a hundred essays, that difference becomes a new way of thinking.
ch.cap: A galloping servant hurls Montaigne from his horse

ch.h: A ceiling built to keep him humble
b: In 1568 his father died and Michel inherited the estate. On his thirty-eighth birthday, 28 February 1571, he formally retired from public life, and had a Latin inscription painted on the wall of his study to say so: he was withdrawing, long weary of the servitude of the courts and public office, into the bosom of the learned Muses, to spend what remained of his life in peace.

He settled into the round tower at a corner of his château. On the ground floor was a chapel, above it a bedroom, and at the top a library of around a thousand books, with windows looking out over the courtyard and the land. Then he had the ceiling beams painted with dozens of sayings in Latin and Greek: lines from Ecclesiastes, Lucretius and Horace, and many from Sextus Empiricus, the ancient compiler of radical doubt. He could not look up from his reading without being told that certainty is not on offer.
A few years later, in 1576, he had a medal struck. On it was a pair of balanced scales and a motto of three words in the French of his day: Que sçay-je? What do I know?

Notice what he did. He did not simply resolve to be humble. He arranged his surroundings so that arrogance became inconvenient. Conviction, he understood, is a default setting, and it has to be designed against.

His plan for retirement was modest: to let his mind rest and amuse itself. Instead, he says, it bolted like a runaway horse, throwing up so many strange monsters and fantasies that he began writing them down, hoping in time to make it ashamed of itself. That was the beginning of the Essays.
ch.cap: Montaigne reads beneath beams painted with doubting sayings

b: He sat down meaning, more or less, to write like the Romans he loved: Seneca's letters, Plutarch's lives. What came out had no name, so he gave it one. He called the pieces essais, from the French essayer, to try, to attempt, to test a metal to see what it is made of. Today an essay means a formal argument, almost the opposite of what he meant. He meant a trial run. A piece of thinking not yet finished.

The form came from a conviction about the subject. Montaigne did not believe the self was a fixed thing that could be described once and filed away. He thought it was always moving, so any portrait of it had to move too. I do not portray being, he wrote. I portray passing.

So when he changed his mind, he did not delete his old opinion. He left it in and added the new thought beside it. The first two books came out in Bordeaux in 1580. A third book and hundreds of additions followed in 1588. He kept writing corrections in the margins of his own copy until he died, and those became the edition of 1595. The result has layers like rock: one man disagreeing with himself across twenty years, in public, without embarrassment.

Nobody had written like this before. It suggests a useful habit: keep a decision journal his way. When you make a real call, write what you expect, what you are assuming and how confident you are. Six months later, write what happened underneath, without editing the original. Within a couple of years you will know which kinds of judgement you are good at and which you should stop making alone.
ch.cap: Montaigne adds new thoughts beside his old ones

ch.h: Who knows if the cat is playing with me?
b: The intellectual centre of the Essays is a long, strange essay called the Apology for Raymond Sebond. It began as a defence of a fifteenth-century theologian whose book Montaigne had translated at his father's request, and it turns into the most thorough demolition of human intellectual confidence of its age.

His method is accumulation. He heaps up the variety of human belief: what different peoples find shameful, what different authorities claim to have proved, how differently the same man judges the same question before and after dinner. He keeps going until your confidence gives way. He is especially hard on our ranking of ourselves above the animals. When I play with my cat, he writes, who knows whether she is not passing her time with me more than I with her?

This scepticism is not despair. It has three practical results. The first is tolerance. From 1562 France was torn by wars of religion between Catholics and Protestants, and Montaigne saw people tortured and killed over doctrine. His point is that the confidence with which people kill each other is never matched by the evidence any of them actually have.

The second is custom. If reason cannot deliver certainty, what do you live by? Mostly, he says, by the laws and habits you already have, not because they are right, but because tearing them up on the strength of a theory usually costs more than their faults. The third is attention. If you cannot know the world, you can at least study one specimen of it closely, and you have private access to exactly one.
ch.cap: Montaigne plays with his cat, or she plays with him

b: In 1562 three Tupinambá men from Brazil were brought to Rouen and presented to the twelve-year-old King Charles IX. Everyone stared at them. Montaigne, by his own account, talked to them, through an interpreter he complained was too stupid to follow his questions.

He asked what they thought of France. They had noticed, one said, that there were men gorged with every good thing, while their other halves, as they called fellow human beings, begged at their doors, thin with hunger. They found it strange that the hungry put up with this rather than taking the others by the throat or setting fire to their houses. Montaigne asked one of them, a leader, what advantage he got from his rank at home. To march first into war, came the answer.

In the essay Of Cannibals he describes their society, including the eating of enemies killed in war, and then turns the telescope round. They eat the dead, he observes. We tear living men apart on the rack, roast them by degrees and set dogs on them, and we have done it recently, among neighbours and fellow citizens, under cover of piety and religion. There is more barbarity, he concludes, in eating a man alive than in eating him dead.

Two cautions. Montaigne is not really doing anthropology. He uses the Tupinambá as a mirror for a French argument about French cruelty, and the noble savage tradition he helped launch did its own damage. But the move itself, asking what we look like from outside, was genuinely new, and it is still the best way to see your own assumptions. Shakespeare read the essay in John Florio's 1603 translation and borrowed from it for Gonzalo's speech in The Tempest.
ch.cap: Three Tupinambá men face the boy king at Rouen

ch.h: A body that will not be ignored
b: Montaigne read everything the Stoics wrote. He adored Seneca and Plutarch and plundered them for quotations. And in the end he broke with them on a point of fact. He did not believe their perfect sage, untroubled by pain and indifferent to his body, had ever existed, and he thought pretending otherwise was bad for people.

His evidence was his own body, about which he was more candid than any writer before modern times. From 1578 he suffered from kidney stones, which in the sixteenth century meant passing gravel in agony without anaesthetic. He describes the attacks in clinical detail. He writes about his digestion, his sleep, his poor memory, what he likes to eat and how he prefers to ride, and, in one notorious passage, about impotence and the comedy of sex.

In 1580, with the first edition just printed, he set off on a long journey through Switzerland and Germany to Italy, partly in search of spa waters that might ease the stones. His travel journal records his gravel alongside churches and conversations. He was taking the waters near Lucca in September 1581 when news arrived that would end the trip.

None of this candour is confession for its own sake. It is an argument. A philosophy that tells you to be indifferent to the body is addressed to a creature that does not exist, because the real creature has a body that shapes his mood, his judgement and even his virtue on any given afternoon. Every man, Montaigne wrote, bears the whole form of the human condition. Examine one ordinary man honestly, and everyone will recognise themselves.
Where the Stoics want you to rise above your nature, Montaigne wants you to learn its shape and arrange your life to fit it. If you are irritable before lunch, hold the hard conversation after it.
ch.cap: Taking the waters near Lucca, Montaigne gets urgent news

ch.h: Mayor in a time of war and plague
b: The news was that the citizens of Bordeaux had elected him mayor, in his absence and without asking. He tried to decline. A letter from King Henri III told him, politely, to come home at once and do his duty. He served two terms, from 1581 to 1585.

It was not a quiet job. The wars of religion were still burning, and Bordeaux was a Catholic city in a region full of Protestants. Montaigne, a Catholic trusted by both sides, acted as a go-between for the Protestant leader Henri of Navarre, the future King Henri IV, and the royal court. That role only works if both sides trust you.

His record has one blot his critics never let go. In 1585, at the very end of his term, plague broke out in Bordeaux. Montaigne was outside the city, and rather than return to hand over office in person, he stayed away. Then the plague reached his own estate, and for months he wandered with his family in search of shelter.

In 1588, in Paris to see a new edition through the press, he was arrested by the Catholic League and thrown into the Bastille, apparently in retaliation for the king's arrest of one of their own. He was released the same evening after the queen mother, Catherine de' Medici, intervened.
So the charge that he hid in his tower while France burned is weaker than it sounds. He did the public work, and declined to pretend it achieved more than it did.
ch.cap: Mayor Montaigne carries messages between the warring camps

ch.h: The foolish project of describing himself
b: Montaigne died at his château on 13 September 1592, aged fifty-nine, after an illness that took away his power of speech. He was still adding notes to the margins of his own copy of the Essays. Marie de Gournay, a young writer who had fallen in love with the book before she met the man, and whom he called his adopted daughter, worked with his widow to publish the full edition in 1595.

Not everyone was charmed. A couple of generations later Blaise Pascal, who had clearly read him closely, attacked the whole enterprise in a phrase that still bites: the foolish project he has of describing himself. Pascal's charge was that self-portraiture is vanity in a scholar's gown, and that suspended judgement is a comfortable bed for a man who does not want to face the questions that matter. The Church eventually agreed, and in 1676 the Essays were placed on the Index of Prohibited Books.

Hold that objection open, because it is real. Self-examination can become a way of avoiding decisions. A useful test is whether your reflection has actually changed something you did in the last month.

But the book outlived its critics, and its legacy is a set of moves you can use every week. Test received wisdom, the Stoics' included, against your own experience. Write corrections underneath, not over. Design around your temperament instead of pretending to rise above it. Turn the telescope round and ask how you look from outside. And keep a little of that painted ceiling in your head, a reminder that the honest answer to most big questions begins with three words: what do I know?
ch.cap: Dying Montaigne still writes in his book's margins

take: Test the doctrine against your life

Montaigne noticed where what happened differed from what the books predicted, and dying turned out easier than the ancients said. Treat received wisdom, this week's included, as a hypothesis about you.
Keep a decision journal with your expectation, assumptions and confidence, and add the outcome below six months later. Within two years you will know which calls you should stop making alone.
He painted doubt on his ceiling rather than resolving to be humble. Build a habit or a person into your routine whose job is to challenge your strongest assumptions.
Scepticism is a tool, not a shrug

His doubt produced tolerance, respect for working customs over untested theories, and close attention to the one specimen he could study. Use what do I know before a big decision, not as an excuse to avoid one.
Log sleep, mood and your hardest daily decision for two weeks. Then put hiring and contract reviews in your best window as a rule, not an intention.
Ask once a quarter how your business looks to the customer who left, the candidate who declined or the supplier you squeeze. It is the most reliable way to see an assumption you cannot otherwise see.
Leave the armour off the people who matter

Epictetus said remind yourself the ones you love are mortal; Montaigne lost La Boétie anyway and judged the protection not worth what it cost. Use detachment on pain and politics, not on your closest people.
Self-examination can turn into vanity or a way to avoid deciding. Check that your reflection changed at least one real decision this month.
recall: What did Montaigne conclude from his riding accident?

That dying needed no preparation: the experience was a gentle drifting, with pain arriving only during recovery. Since the ancients had told men to rehearse for death all their lives, his own evidence suggested the training was aimed at a fear rather than the event.
What does essai mean, and why did Montaigne need a new form?

An attempt or trial, like testing a metal, not a finished argument. He held that the self is always in motion, I portray passing, not being, so he needed an unfinished form and added new opinions beside old ones rather than deleting them.
Name the three practical results Montaigne draws from his scepticism.

Tolerance, because the confidence with which people persecute each other is never matched by their evidence. A preference for existing custom over untested theory, because tearing things up usually costs more. And close attention to the one specimen he could truly examine, himself.
What did the Tupinambá at Rouen say about France, and what point did Montaigne draw?

They were struck that some men were gorged while others begged at their doors, and that the hungry put up with it; their leader said his privilege was to march first into war. Montaigne turned this into a mirror: Europeans torturing the living for religion were more barbarous than people who ate the dead.
How did Pascal attack Montaigne, and what answers the charge that he hid from public life?

Pascal mocked the foolish project of describing himself, calling self-portrait vanity and suspended judgement an evasion; the Essays were put on the Index in 1676. Against hiding: he served two terms as mayor of Bordeaux from 1581 and acted as go-between for Henri of Navarre and the royal court.
note: Main sources are the Essays themselves, Montaigne's travel journal, and biographies such as Sarah Bakewell's How to Live, 2010. The date of the riding accident is uncertain, usually placed around 1569 or 1570. His mother's converso ancestry is widely accepted but debated. Montaigne's presence at Rouen in 1562 rests on his own account, which most scholars accept. The number of ceiling inscriptions varies between counts because some were painted over, so no exact figure is given here.
words: The branch of philosophy that asks what knowledge is and how we can know anything.
The Apology for Raymond Sebond is Montaigne's great work of epistemology, piling up the variety of human belief until confident claims to knowledge give way.
Gradual growth by the addition of new layers over time.
The Essays grew by accretion: Montaigne kept old opinions in place and added new ones beside them across twenty years, so the text has layers like rock.
Judging other cultures by the standards of your own and assuming yours is superior.
In Of Cannibals Montaigne turns ethnocentrism on its head, arguing that French torture under cover of religion was more barbaric than the Tupinambá eating their dead.
To forbid or condemn something officially.
In 1676 the Church proscribed the Essays by placing them on the Index of Prohibited Books, partly on the charge Pascal had pressed against self-portraiture.
A person who takes part in a conversation or acts as a go-between in one.
Montaigne treats his reader as a private interlocutor rather than an audience, and as mayor he served as a trusted interlocutor between the Catholic court and the Protestant Henri of Navarre.

biz: Keep a decision journal for marketing

Montaigne wrote new thoughts beside old ones instead of over them. Do the same with campaign and website decisions. Each time you suggest a change for Grok to action in Google or Bing, or approve a new landing page or SEO article, write one line: what you expect to happen, by when, what you are assuming, and how confident you are, for example cost per qualified lead down fifteen per cent in six weeks, sixty per cent confident. Six weeks later write what happened underneath, without editing the original. Within a year you will know which of your instincts to trust and which calls to stop making alone.
Turn the telescope round on your customer journey

Montaigne asked what France looked like through Brazilian eyes. Ask what HomeownersLoan and Debt Support Direct look like through the eyes of a frightened homeowner reading on a phone at midnight. This week, have someone outside the business complete an enquiry on each site and read every WhatsApp message they receive. Ask them three questions: what do you think will happen next, what will it cost you, and did anything feel pushy or confusing? That is Consumer Duty's consumer understanding outcome tested in practice. Fix the top three answers they get wrong, then repeat with a new person every quarter.
connects: Montaigne's habit of recording a view and then writing the correction beneath it is a forerunner of Tetlock's forecasters, who keep score of their own predictions and update in small honest steps.
Montaigne watched Catholics and Protestants kill each other with more confidence than evidence, the same moral certainty Haidt explains as intuition first and reasoning afterwards.
Taleb's scepticism about what experts can know descends directly from the radical doubt Montaigne had painted on his ceiling beams from Sextus Empiricus.
recap:
Michel de Montaigne was born in the year fifteen thirty-three, at a château east of Bordeaux, into a family that had climbed from selling wine and salted fish into the minor nobility. His father treated him as an experiment. The baby was nursed among peasants, woken each morning by music, and raised speaking Latin before French, because the whole household was ordered to speak only Latin to him.

He became a magistrate, and there he met Étienne de La Boétie. They were friends at once and completely, and within five years La Boétie was dead. Asked why he loved him, Montaigne could only say: because it was he, because it was I. Some think the Essays exist to fill that silence.

Then a servant galloping too fast crashed into him on a country path, and Montaigne nearly died. What struck him was that it did not feel terrible. It felt like drifting. The books had said one thing, and his own experience said another. That gap became his method.

At thirty-eight he retired to a round tower full of books and painted the ceiling beams with sayings about the limits of knowledge. He had a medal struck with three words: what do I know? He did not just decide to be humble. He designed his surroundings so that arrogance was inconvenient.

Out of that tower came a new form. He called the pieces essays, attempts, trial runs. He believed the self was always moving, so when he changed his mind he left the old view in and added the new one beside it.

His big ideas are easy to carry. First, doubt your certainties, because in his France people were tortured over doctrines nobody could prove. Second, turn the telescope round. After meeting three Brazilian men at Rouen, he asked who the real barbarians were, the people who ate the dead or the people who tortured the living. Third, take the body seriously. He wrote openly about kidney stones and digestion, because a philosophy that ignores the body is addressed to nobody. Fourth, test every piece of wisdom, even the Stoics, against your own life.

He was dragged back to serve as mayor of Bordeaux during war and plague, and did the work without pretending it achieved more than it did. Pascal mocked his foolish project of describing himself, and the Church banned the book. It outlived them all.

The line to remember: the honest answer to most big questions begins with what do I know?
